explain: Git is one command with subcommands: git add, git commit, git push. After that, the usual flags and arguments.

syntax: working folder  →  git add  →  staging  →  git commit  →  history
explain: The three places: your files, the staging area (what goes in the next commit), and the history of commits.
remember: Edit, add (pack the box), commit (seal the box).

syntax:
git push origin main
git pull origin main
explain: Remotes: origin is the name of the copy on GitHub; main is the branch. push sends commits up, pull brings them down.
remember: push up, pull down, origin = GitHub.

syntax:
git switch -c new-idea
git switch main
explain: A branch is a named line of commits. -c creates one.
example: Trying an idea without breaking main.
remember: Branch = a parallel line of history.

explain: Subcommand (commit) + flag (-m) + argument (the message in quotes).
Subcommand (log) + a long flag + a short flag with a number.
remember: Read flags as adjectives: short, last 5.

explain: Tells Git your name. It goes on every commit you make. Do it once per computer.
Tells Git your email. Use the same email as your GitHub account so commits link to you.
example: The email on your GitHub account.

explain: Turns the current folder into a Git project (a repository). Git starts watching its files.
example: Start tracking a brand new project.

explain: Downloads a whole project from GitHub, with all its history, into a new folder.
Shows which files changed, which are ready to commit, and which branch you are on. Run it often.
example: Check what changed before you commit.

explain: Shows exactly which lines changed that are not added yet.
example: Read your changes before saving them.

explain: Shows the changes you already added, which will go into the next commit.
Lists past commits, one per line: a short id and the message.
example: See the history of the project.

explain: Shows what one commit changed.
Puts one file in the "ready to commit" area (the staging area).
Adds every changed file in this folder and below.
Saves a snapshot of the added files, with a short message saying what you did.
Changes the message of your last commit. Only do this before you push.
example: Fix a typo in the last commit message.

explain: Shows which GitHub address this project is connected to.
example: Check where git push sends your work.

explain: Connects a local project to an empty GitHub repository. "origin" is the usual name for it.
Sends your new commits to GitHub.
The first push of a new branch: sends it and remembers where it goes, so next time plain git push works.
example: The first push of a new project.

explain: Gets new commits from GitHub and adds them to your branch.
example: Get changes you made on another computer.

explain: Downloads news from GitHub but does not change your files yet.
example: See if anything new is there before pulling.

explain: Lists your branches. The * marks the one you are on.
Makes a new branch and moves to it. Try ideas there without touching main.
Moves to another branch. Your files change to match it.
Brings the commits from another branch into the branch you are on.
Deletes a branch you already merged.
Throws away the changes in a file that you have not added yet. They cannot come back.
Takes a file out of the "ready to commit" area. Your changes stay in the file.
example: Added the wrong file? Un-add it.

explain: Makes a new commit that undoes an old one. Safe even after you pushed.
stash puts your unfinished changes away; stash pop brings them back.
example: Switch branches without committing half-done work.

explain: A file listing things Git should never track, one per line.

syntax:
git status
git add .
git commit -m "message"
git push
explain: The everyday loop: check, add, save, send to GitHub.
example: After finishing a small piece of work.
